title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
openingChapterLabel: Part I, Chapter 1 — The Oblonsky household
openingText: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
about:
Anna Karenina is two novels braided together. In one, Anna — the brilliant, beautiful wife of a senior Petersburg official — meets the cavalry officer Count Vronsky at a Moscow train station and walks out of her marriage to live with him. In the other, Konstantin Levin — a landowner in his thirties, awkward and earnest — fails at proposing to the eighteen-year-old Princess Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, retreats to his estate to think, and slowly works his way back toward her and toward a life he can defend. The two stories cross at a few hinges and never merge. Tolstoy puts them next to each other and lets the reader compare.

Tolstoy began the novel in 1873 and finished it in 1877. He was in his late forties, recently a father several times over, and starting to feel the religious crisis that would later produce A Confession. The book was serialized in The Russian Messenger over four years; the editor refused to publish the final part because of its hostile view of Russia's war in the Balkans, and Tolstoy published Part 8 separately as a pamphlet. The novel runs to roughly 800 pages and tracks its characters through marriages, infidelities, childbirths, a steeplechase, hunting trips, provincial elections, a death in a hotel room, and a religious conversion.

It is the novel Tolstoy himself most wanted to be remembered for, and the one writers from Faulkner to Nabokov have called the greatest ever written. The first sentence is the most quoted opening in fiction. The last hundred pages — Levin alone with God and his crops — are autobiography in everything but name.

angleCards.title: Anna's story.
angleCards.text: Follow Anna from the moment she steps off the Moscow train and meets Vronsky on the platform. Watch how the affair begins, how Petersburg society accepts it and then turns on her, and what is left of her by the time she returns to that same station.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Anna's arc from her arrival in Moscow to her final return to the train station — how the affair begins, what society does to her, and what she does to herself.

angleCards.title: Levin's story.
angleCards.text: The other half of the novel is Levin: the awkward landowner trying to figure out how to propose to Kitty, how to run his estate, and whether life is worth living without God. Tolstoy gave him his own thinking. The last chapter is Levin's answer.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Levin as Tolstoy's stand-in: track his proposal to Kitty, his quarrel with the new Russia, and the religious answer he finally reaches in the last chapter.

angleCards.title: The two marriages.
angleCards.text: Tolstoy puts Anna and Vronsky's affair next to Levin and Kitty's marriage on purpose. The novel never tells you what to conclude. It just shows you what each path costs and what each path gives, in alternating chapters, for eight hundred pages.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Anna-Vronsky and Levin-Kitty plots as a structured comparison of two ways of loving, and decide what Tolstoy thinks each path costs and gives.

angleCards.title: Happy families are alike.
angleCards.text: The most famous opening sentence in fiction is the thesis of the whole book. Tolstoy then spends eight hundred pages testing it: showing exactly how the Oblonskys, the Karenins, and the Levins are each unhappy in their own way, and what — if anything — keeps the Levins from joining the other two.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track Tolstoy's opening claim — happy families are alike, unhappy families each unhappy in their own way — across the three marriages, and see whether the book actually defends it.

cast.name: Anna Arkadyevna Karenina
cast.description: A handsome, intelligent Petersburg society wife in her late twenties, married eight years to a senior government official twenty years her elder. She has one son, Seryozha, whom she adores. She arrives in Moscow in Part 1 to broker peace in her brother Stiva's marriage; on the platform she meets Count Vronsky. The novel is the story of what she does next, what Petersburg lets her do, and what it does to her when she stops hiding.

cast.name: Count Alexey Kirillovich Vronsky
cast.description: A wealthy young cavalry officer, a few years younger than Anna, with a promising military career and no settled plans. He is courting Kitty Shtcherbatskaya — without any clear intention of marrying her — when he sees Anna and abandons that courtship. He is honorable by the rules of his class and decisively dishonorable by any other measure. He gives up his career for Anna and discovers, slowly, that the life he has chosen with her does not have enough in it to fill a day.

cast.name: Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin
cast.description: Anna's husband: a senior government minister twenty years her elder, eminent, austere, and constitutionally unable to express feeling. The novel makes him neither a villain nor a fool. He is competent at his job and helpless at his marriage. When the affair becomes public, he behaves correctly, then religiously, then cruelly — usually under the influence of someone louder than he is. His suffering is one of the surprises of the book.

cast.name: Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin
cast.description: A landowner in his early thirties, awkward in society and serious in person, who manages his family's estate and writes a book on Russian agriculture. He comes to Moscow in Part 1 to propose to Princess Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, is refused, and retreats to the country to brood. Tolstoy gave Levin his own farming, his own marriage, his own brothers, and most of his own religious questions. The novel ends with Levin alone in the garden, working out what to believe.

cast.name: Princess Ekaterina "Kitty" Shtcherbatskaya
cast.description: The youngest of the three Shtcherbatsky sisters, eighteen at the start of the book, recently out in society. She refuses Levin's proposal in Part 1 expecting an offer from Vronsky that does not come; the humiliation makes her physically ill. She is more capable and more clear-sighted than anyone, including her, has noticed. Her care for Levin's dying brother in a provincial hotel is one of the book's quiet turning points.

cast.name: Prince Stepan "Stiva" Oblonsky
cast.description: Anna's older brother and Dolly's husband: handsome, charming, perpetually in debt, and incapable of taking anything seriously. The novel opens on him: his wife has just discovered he is sleeping with the governess, and the family is in chaos. He moves through the book lightly while everyone around him pays for his choices — and is, somehow, the character no one is able to hate.

acclaim.quote: Anna Karenina is perfection as a work of art … and one with which nothing of the like in European literature in our day can be compared.

acclaim.context: on Anna Karenina, Faulkner in the University seminars, University of Virginia, 1957–58

acclaim.quote: Tolstoy is the greatest Russian writer of prose fiction.
acclaim.context: Lectures on Russian Literature, lecture on Tolstoy, delivered at Cornell 1948–58, published 1981

whyItMatters.title: The Most Quoted Opening in Fiction
whyItMatters.body: "All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." Tolstoy spends the next eight hundred pages testing the sentence. The Oblonskys are unhappy because Stiva cannot stop sleeping with other women and Dolly cannot stop loving him; the Karenins are unhappy because Karenin cannot express anything and Anna can no longer live inside her marriage; the Levins are not yet a family at the start, and the novel watches Konstantin and Kitty try to become one. Each of these unhappinesses has its own engine, its own vocabulary, its own daily texture. The single sentence at the front of the book is not decoration — it is the thesis. The novel is the test. Tolstoy doesn't tell you whether the thesis holds. He shows you three families and lets you decide.

whyItMatters.title: A Society That Allows, Then Destroys
whyItMatters.body: Petersburg society in 1875 does not punish Anna for the affair. It punishes her for refusing to hide it. Princess Betsy and her circle conduct identical affairs in plain sight; the rule is that everyone knows and nobody says. When Anna stops attending the right salons with the right people, when she appears at the opera with Vronsky as though she were his wife, the same women who covered for Betsy turn on her. Tolstoy lays the social mechanism out coldly: who speaks to her, who stops speaking to her, who invites her, who is suddenly busy. By the end she is alone in a country house with Vronsky, and the loneliness is unbearable. The novel was published almost fifty years before Madame Bovary received a sympathetic reading and a hundred years before "the male gaze" entered English. Tolstoy is doing all of it, in 1877, without naming any of it.

whyItMatters.title: Tolstoy's Religious Crisis in Real Time
whyItMatters.body: Levin spends the novel trying to find a reason not to kill himself. He hides his rope and his gun from himself. He has a successful estate, a wife he loves, a healthy son; he is also, in his own description, on the edge of suicide for most of Part 8. The crisis is not Levin's; it is Tolstoy's. He was writing the novel through the same religious collapse that would, two years after publication, produce A Confession and break him as a novelist. The last twenty pages of Anna Karenina — Levin alone in the garden, on the path, in the storm with the baby — are Tolstoy working out, in real time, the answer he would spend the rest of his life trying to live by. The answer arrives in a single sentence from a peasant about another peasant: that some men live for their belly, and some live for their soul, for God. Levin recognizes it as something he already knew and could not put into words. Tolstoy never wrote another novel.
